title: Phase coherence control of a programmable high-Tc superconductor created by light
hook: For 50+ years physicists chased superconductivity switched on by light — now a laser can write it, dial its temperature up or down, and erase it again, like a dimmer switch.
key_points: The quest for light-induced superconductivity has run over 50 years without direct proof it could be created and controlled.
Physicists made a 'light-programmable superconducting' (LiPS) state at an aluminum-silicon interface with femtosecond laser pulses.
Tailored light-pulse sequences raise or erase the superconducting critical temperature (1.8-8.5 K) at will.
The effect comes from light controlling a moiré-like superlattice of lattice-mismatch dislocations at the interface.
The state behaves as effectively two-dimensional, showing vortex pinning and creep under a magnetic field.
It points toward light-'written' superconducting circuits and tunable quantum-processor components.
content_html: Physicists have chased the idea of switching superconductivity on with light for more than fifty years, but no one had directly shown a zero-resistance state that light could both create and fully control — until now. A team has built exactly that: a superconductor you can dial up, down, or erase with tailored laser pulses, like a dimmer switch.
extra_html: Viktoria Yursa, Igor Vaskivskyi, Dragan Mihailovic, and colleagues created the effect — dubbed LiPS, for light-programmable superconductivity — at an aluminum-silicon interface using femtosecond laser pulses. The superconducting critical temperature, tunable between 1.8 and 8.5 Kelvin, can be raised or erased just by changing the light-pulse sequence. The team traces the effect to light controlling a moiré-like pattern of tiny lattice-mismatch dislocations that naturally form where aluminum meets silicon, visible under high-resolution electron microscopy. Under a magnetic field, the material behaves like an effectively two-dimensional superconductor. The authors say the demonstration opens a path toward locally "writing" superconducting circuits or tuning quantum processors with light.

related.title: Superconductivity: Electricity with Zero Resistance
related.hook: Cool certain materials cold enough and their electrical resistance vanishes completely. A current set flowing in a loop would, in principle, circle forever without fading.

related.title: AI Just Helped Find Two New Superconductors
related.hook: Machine learning helped physicists find two new superconductors and sketch a faster route toward physics' biggest prize in the field: a superconductor that works at room temperature.

flashcards.prompt: What is new about the 'light-programmable superconducting' (LiPS) state reported here?
flashcards.back_html: It's the first zero-resistance state whose critical temperature can be both created and fully controlled — raised or erased at will — using tailored laser pulses.

flashcards.prompt: What causes the LiPS effect, according to the researchers?

choices.text: Light controlling a moiré-like superlattice of lattice-mismatch dislocations at the interface
A chemical reaction between the aluminum and silicon atoms
Cooling the material to near absolute zero

flashcards.explanation_html: The dislocation superlattice that naturally forms between the aluminum and silicon lattices is what light pulses tune to switch superconductivity on or off.

flashcards.prompt: How is the LiPS state's critical temperature controlled?
flashcards.back_html: By applying different tailored sequences of femtosecond laser pulses — it can be raised or erased at will, across a range of 1.8 to 8.5 Kelvin.
